sec.title: 1.1 Asymptotic property of the estimator for A
sec.p: This section derives the asymptotic estimation error of the OLS estimator A^\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}$\end{document} for the system matrix A. The primary goal is to obtain a first-order asymptotic approximation for the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the estimation, quantified by the expected squared Frobenius norm, E[‖A^−A‖F2]\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}[\|\hat {{A}}- {A}\|_{F}^{2}]$\end{document}.

We consider the linear dynamical system(A1.1)x(t+1)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)+ξ(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle {\boldsymbol x}(t+1) = {\boldsymbol A} {\boldsymbol x}(t) + {\boldsymbol B} {\boldsymbol u}(t) + {\boldsymbol \xi }(t),$$\end{document}

where the noise ξ(t)\begin{document}${\boldsymbol \xi }(t)$\end{document} is i.i.d. over time with zero mean and covariance matrix Σξ=E[ξ(t)ξ(t)⊤]∈Rn×n≻0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi } = \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol {\xi }(t)\boldsymbol {\xi }(t)^{\!\top }] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\succ 0$\end{document}.

We estimate A by OLS from the data matrices X∈Rn×T\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {X}\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times T}$\end{document}, Y~:=Y−BU∈Rn×T\begin{document}$\tilde {\boldsymbol {Y}}:= \boldsymbol {Y}- \boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {U}\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times T}$\end{document}, giving A^=Y~X†\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}= \tilde {\boldsymbol {Y}}\boldsymbol {X}^{\dagger }$\end{document}.

The asymptotic distribution of the vectorized estimation error of the OLS estimator A^\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}$\end{document} is given by Hamilton, 1994, Proposition 11.1 and Appendix 11.A:(A1.2)T(vec(A^)−vec(A))→LN(0,ΣAsym),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sqrt{T}\bigl (\mathrm{vec}(\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}) - \mathrm{vec}(\boldsymbol {A})\bigr) \xrightarrow {L}\mathcal{N}\bigl (\boldsymbol {0},\, \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}}\bigr),$$\end{document}

where T is the number of samples, →L\begin{document}$\xrightarrow {L}$\end{document} denotes convergence in distribution, and ΣAsym\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}}$\end{document} is the asymptotic covariance matrix. Following the notation in the original text (and its assumptions), this covariance is:(A1.3)ΣAsym=Σξ⊗ΣX−1,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}}= \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi } \otimes \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\boldsymbol {X}}^{-1},$$\end{document}

where ⊗\begin{document}$\otimes $\end{document} denotes the Kronecker product [Hamilton, 1994, Appendix A.4, p.732], Σξ∈Rn×n\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi } \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$\end{document} is the noise covariance, and ΣX=E[x(t)x(t)⊤]∈Rn×n\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\boldsymbol {X}}= \mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol {x}(t)\boldsymbol {x}(t)^{\top }] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$\end{document} is the state covariance matrix, so that ΣAsym∈Rn2×n2\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}}\in \mathbb{R}^{n^2 \times n^2}$\end{document}.

We are interested in the estimation error measured by the squared Frobenius norm, ‖A^−A‖F2\begin{document}$\|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2}$\end{document}. Let us define the normalized error vector zT\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}_{T}$\end{document} based on (Equation A1.2):(A1.4)zT:=T(vec(A^)−vec(A)).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {z}_{T} := \sqrt{T}\bigl (\mathrm{vec}(\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}) - \mathrm{vec}(\boldsymbol {A})\bigr).$$\end{document}

We know that zT→Lz\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}_{T} \xrightarrow {L}\boldsymbol {z}$\end{document}, where z∼N(0,ΣAsym)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}\sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol {0}, \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}})$\end{document} is an n2\begin{document}$n^{2}$\end{document}-dimensional Gaussian vector.

The squared Frobenius norm can be expressed as the squared Euclidean norm of the vectorized error:(A1.5)‖A^−A‖F2=‖vec(A^−A)‖22.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2} = \|\mathrm{vec}(\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A})\|_{2}^{2}.$$\end{document}

Multiplying by T, we can relate this quantity to zT\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}_{T}$\end{document}:(A1.6)T⋅‖A^−A‖F2=(T⋅‖vec(A^−A)‖2)2=zT⊤zT.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle T \cdot \|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2} = \left (\sqrt{T}\cdot \|\mathrm{vec}(\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A})\|_{2}\right)^{2} = \boldsymbol {z}_{T}^{\top } \boldsymbol {z}_{T}.$$\end{document}

By the continuous mapping theorem, since g(z)=z⊤z\begin{document}$g(\boldsymbol {z}) = \boldsymbol {z}^{\top } \boldsymbol {z}$\end{document} is a continuous function, the convergence in distribution of zT\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}_{T}$\end{document} implies the convergence in distribution of zT⊤zT\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}_{T}^{\top } \boldsymbol {z}_{T}$\end{document}:(A1.7)T⋅‖A^−A‖F2→Lz⊤z,wherez∼N(0,ΣAsym).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle T \cdot \|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2} \xrightarrow {L}\boldsymbol {z}^{\top } \boldsymbol {z}, \quad \text{where}\quad \boldsymbol {z}\sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol {0}, \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}}).$$\end{document}

Its limit of the expected value equals the expectation of the limiting distribution z⊤z\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {z}^{\top } \boldsymbol {z}$\end{document}:(A1.8)limT→∞E[T⋅‖A^−A‖F2]=E[z⊤z]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \lim _{T \to \infty }\mathbb{E}\!\left [T \cdot \|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2}\right ] = \mathbb{E}\!\left [\boldsymbol {z}^{\top } \boldsymbol {z}\right ]$$\end{document}(A1.9)=E[tr(zz⊤)]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \mathbb{E}\!\left [\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {z}\boldsymbol {z}^{\top })\right ]$$\end{document}(A1.10)=tr(E[zz⊤]).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \mathrm{tr}\!\left (\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol {z}\boldsymbol {z}^{\top }]\right).$$\end{document}

By definition, E[zz⊤]\begin{document}$\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol {z}\boldsymbol {z}^{\top }]$\end{document} is the covariance matrix of the limiting distribution z, which is ΣAsym\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}}$\end{document}.(A1.11)limT→∞E[T⋅‖A^−A‖F2]=tr(ΣAsym)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \lim _{T \to \infty }\mathbb{E}\!\left [T \cdot \|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2}\right ] = \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\mathrm{Asym}})$$\end{document}(A1.12)=tr(Σξ⊗ΣX−1).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi } \otimes \boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\boldsymbol {X}}^{-1}).$$\end{document}

Using the trace property tr(A⊗B)=tr(A)tr(B)\begin{document}$\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {A}\otimes \boldsymbol {B}) = \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {A})\,\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {B})$\end{document}, we obtain:(A1.13)limT→∞E[T⋅‖A^−A‖F2]=tr(Σξ)tr(ΣX−1).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \lim _{T \to \infty }\mathbb{E}\!\left [T \cdot \|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2}\right ] = \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi })\,\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\boldsymbol {X}}^{-1}).$$\end{document}

This result implies that for a sufficiently large T, the expected estimation error can be approximated as:(A1.14)E[‖A^−A‖F2]≈1Ttr(Σξ)tr(ΣX−1).\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \mathbb{E}\!\left [\|\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}- \boldsymbol {A}\|_{F}^{2}\right ] \approx \frac{1}{T}\,\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi })\,\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\boldsymbol {X}}^{-1}).$$\end{document}

This expression provides a simple interpretation of the estimation error. It confirms that the error is inversely proportional to the sample size T, meaning the error decreases as more data is collected. The error is also directly proportional to the total noise power, tr(Σξ)\begin{document}$\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\xi })$\end{document}, indicating that more noise leads to more error. Furthermore, the error is proportional to tr(ΣX−1)\begin{document}$\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol {\Sigma }_{\boldsymbol {X}}^{-1})$\end{document}, which acts as an inverse measure of signal strength; a weaker signal x(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}(t)$\end{document} (i.e. less variation) leads to a larger error. This relationship resembles the inverse of the Signal-to-Noise ratio, where the error is governed by the balance between noise, signal strength, and the amount of data.

sec.title: 1.2 State vectors considering typical inputs used in neuroscience
1.2.1 Sinusoidal Input
sec.p: To determine which frequencies most effectively enhance system identification accuracy, we now analyze the time evolution of the state vector x(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}(t)$\end{document} in response to a sinusoidal input. This analysis is the necessary first step towards the goal established in the main text (i.e. sufficiently exciting the system’s dynamics to increase the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix). By understanding how x(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}(t)$\end{document} itself behaves under different frequencies, we can identify which inputs are most effective. We, therefore, examine frequency external inputs, represented in neuroscience by tACS, to derive the optimal input frequency based on the system’s dynamic response.

In the case where the perturbation consists of a composite sinusoidal input comprising multiple frequencies, the input can be written as(A1.15)u(k)=∑l=1Lcos⁡(ωlk)u0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {u}(k) = \sum _{l=1}^{L}\cos (\omega _{l} k)\boldsymbol {u}_{0},$$\end{document}
where ωl\begin{document}$\omega _{l}$\end{document} are the angular frequencies.

The general solution which we denote as Equation 10 is:(A1.16)x(t)=Atx(0)+∑k=0t−1At−1−kBu(k)+∑k=0t−1At−1−kξ(k)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}(t) = \boldsymbol {A}^{t} \boldsymbol {x}(0) + \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}(k) + \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {\xi }(k)$$\end{document}

Inserting Equation A1.15 into Equation 10 yields:(A1.17)x(t)=Atx(0)+∑k=0t−1At−1−kB∑l=1Lcos⁡(ωlk)u0+∑k=0t−1At−1−kξ(k)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}(t) = \boldsymbol {A}^{t} \boldsymbol {x}(0) + \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {B}\sum _{l=1}^{L}\cos (\omega _{l} k)\boldsymbol {u}_{0} + \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {\xi }(k)$$\end{document}

Under the assumption that the system is stable (all eigenvalues λd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d}$\end{document} of A satisfy |λd|<1\begin{document}$|\lambda _{d}| \lt 1$\end{document}), the second term of Equation A1.17 is the critical component to analyze.

By performing diagonalization of A as A=VΛV−1\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {A}= \boldsymbol {V}\boldsymbol {\Lambda }\boldsymbol {V}^{-1}$\end{document}, where V is the matrix of eigenvectors, Λ\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {\Lambda }$\end{document} is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues λd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d}$\end{document},... = \frac{1}{2}\sum _{l=1}^{L}\sum _{d=1}^{n}\left (\frac{(r_{d}^{\,t}e^{i\theta _dt}-e^{i\omega _l t})(r_{d}e^{-i\theta _d}-e^{-i\omega _l})}{(r_{d}e^{i\theta _d}-e^{i\omega _l})(r_{d}e^{-i\theta For brevity, we define the following terms:(A1.28)Q(ωl,θd)=rdt+1eiθd(t−1)−rdtei(θdt−ωl)−rdei(ωlt−θd)+eiωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(θd−ωl)+1\begin{document}$$\displaystyle Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})= \frac{r_{d}^{t+1}e^{i\theta _d(t-1)}-r_{d}^{t}e^{i(\theta _dt-\omega _l)}-r_{d}e^{i(\omega _l t-\theta _d)}+e^{i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\theta _{d}-\omega _{l})+1}$$\end{document}(A1.29)Fd=vdwd⊤Bu0\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {F}_{d} = \boldsymbol {v}_{d}\boldsymbol {w}_{d}^{\top }\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$$\end{document}

The second term is:(A1.30)∑k=0t−1At−1−kB∑l=1Lcos⁡(ωlk)u0=12∑l=1L∑d=1n(Q(ωl,θd)+Q(−ωl,θd))Fd\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sum_{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol{A}^{\,t-1-k}\boldsymbol{B}\,\sum_{l=1}^{L}\cos(\omega_l k)\boldsymbol{u}_0 = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{d=1}^{n}\left(Q(\omega_l,\theta_d)+Q(-\omega_l,\theta_d)\right)\boldsymbol{F}_d$$\end{document}

Since the matrix A is real, its complex eigenvalues and eigenvectors must appear in complex conjugate pairs. If λd=rdeiθd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d} = r_{d} e^{i\theta _d}$\end{document} (with θd≠0\begin{document}$\theta _{d} \neq 0$\end{document}) is an eigenvalue, then λd′=λd¯=rde−iθd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d'}= \overline {\lambda _d}= r_{d} e^{-i\theta _d}$\end{document} is also an eigenvalue for some index d′\begin{document}$d'$\end{document}. Thus, θd′=−θd\begin{document}$\theta _{d'}= -\theta _{d}$\end{document}. Furthermore, since B and u0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$\end{document} are also real, the vector Fd=vdwd⊤Bu0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {F}_{d} = \boldsymbol {v}_{d}\boldsymbol {w}_{d}^{\top }\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$\end{document} associated with λd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d}$\end{document} and the vector Fd′=vd′wd′⊤Bu0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}= \boldsymbol {v}_{d'}\boldsymbol {w}_{d'}^{\top }\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$\end{document} associated with λd′\begin{document}$\lambda _{d'}$\end{document} are also complex conjugates: Fd′=Fd¯\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}= \overline {\boldsymbol {F}_d}$\end{document}. We can use this property to simplify the sum.(A1.31)Q(−ωl,θd′)Fd′=Q(−ωl,−θd)Fd¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d'}) \boldsymbol {F}_{d'} = Q(-\omega _{l},-\theta _{d})\overline {\boldsymbol {F}_d}$$\end{document}(A1.32)=rdt+1e−iθd(t−1)−rdtei(−θdt+ωl)−rdei(−ωlt+θd)+e−iωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(−θd+ωl)+1Fd¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \frac{r_{d}^{t+1}e^{-i\theta _d(t-1)}-r_{d}^{t}e^{i(-\theta _dt+\omega _l)}-r_{d}e^{i(-\omega _l t+\theta _d)}+e^{-i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (-\theta _{d}+\omega _{l})+1}\overline {\boldsymbol {F}_d}$$\end{document}(A1.33)=rdt+1eiθd(t−1)−rdtei(θdt−ωl)−rdei(ωlt−θd)+eiωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(θd−ωl)+1Fd¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \overline {\frac{r_{d}^{t+1}e^{i\theta _d(t-1)}-r_{d}^{t}e^{i(\theta _dt-\omega _l)}-r_{d}e^{i(\omega _l t-\theta _d)}+e^{i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\theta _{d}-\omega _{l})+1}\boldsymbol {F}_d}$$\end{document}(A1.34)=Q(ωl,θd)Fd¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \overline {Q(\omega _l, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_d}$$\end{document}
Similarly, Q(−ωl,θd)Fd=Q(ωl,θd′)Fd′¯\begin{document}$Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d} = \overline {Q(\omega _l, \theta _{d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}}$\end{document}

For real eigenvalues (θd=0\begin{document}$\theta _{d}=0$\end{document}), Fd\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {F}_{d}$\end{document} is real, and we find:(A1.35)Q(−ωl,0)Fd=rdt+1−rdteiωl−rde−iωlt+e−iωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(ωl)+1Fd\begin{document}$$\displaystyle Q(-\omega _{l}, 0) \boldsymbol {F}_{d} = \frac{r_{d}^{t+1}-r_{d}^{t}e^{i\omega _l}-r_{d}e^{-i\omega _l t}+e^{-i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\omega _{l})+1}\boldsymbol {F}_{d}$$\end{document}(A1.36)=rdt+1−rdte−iωl−rdeiωlt+eiωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(ωl)+1Fd¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \overline {\frac{r_{d}^{t+1}-r_{d}^{t}e^{-i\omega _l}-r_{d}e^{i\omega _l t}+e^{i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\omega _{l})+1}\boldsymbol {F}_{d}}$$\end{document}(A1.37)=Q(ωl,0)Fd¯\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \overline {Q(\omega _l, 0) \boldsymbol {F}_{d}}$$\end{document}

We divide the set of indices of eigenvalues into three subsets as follows. Let DR\begin{document}$D_{R}$\end{document} denote the set of indices corresponding to real eigenvalues (λd∈R\begin{document}$\lambda _{d} \in \mathbb{R}$\end{document}). Among complex eigenvalues, let DC+\begin{document}$D_{C}^{+}$\end{document} denote the set of indices whose imaginary part is positive, and let DC−\begin{document}$D_{C}^{-}$\end{document} denote the set of indices whose imaginary part is negative.(A1.38)12∑d=1n(Q(ωl,θd)+Q(−ωl,θd))Fd=12∑d∈DR(Q(ωl,0)Fd+Q(ωl,0)Fd¯)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}\sum _{d=1}^{n}\left (Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d}) + Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\right) \boldsymbol {F}_{d} = \frac{1}{2}\sum _{d \in D_R}\left (Q(\omega _{l}, 0)\boldsymbol {F}_{d} + \overline {Q(\omega _l, 0)\boldsymbol {F}_d}\right)$$\end{document}(A1.39)+12∑d∈DC+(Q(ωl,θd)Fd+Q(−ωl,θd)Fd)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle + \frac{1}{2}\sum _{d \in D_C^+}\left (Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d} + Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d} \right)$$\end{document}(A1.40)+12∑d′∈DC−(Q(ωl,θd′)Fd′+Q(−ωl,θd′)Fd′)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle + \frac{1}{2}\sum _{d' \in D_C^-}\left (Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}+ Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}\right)$$\end{document}

Now, we pair the terms from DC+\begin{document}$D_{C}^{+}$\end{document} and DC−\begin{document}$D_{C}^{-}$\end{document}. For each d∈DC+\begin{document}$d \in D_{C}^{+}$\end{document}, there is a corresponding d′∈DC−\begin{document}$d' \in D_{C}^{-}$\end{document} such that θd′=−θd\begin{document}$\theta _{d'}= -\theta _{d}$\end{document} and Fd′=Fd¯\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}= \overline {\boldsymbol {F}_d}$\end{document}. Using the properties Q(−ωl,θd)Fd=Q(ωl,θd′)Fd′¯\begin{document}$Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d} = \overline {Q(\omega _l, \theta _{d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}}$\end{document} and Q(−ωl,θd′)Fd′=Q(ωl,θd)Fd¯\begin{document}$Q(-\omega _{l}, \theta _{d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}= \overline {Q(\omega _l, \theta _d)\boldsymbol {F}_d}$\end{document}, the sum of the DC+\begin{document}$D_{C}^{+}$\end{document} and DC−\begin{document}$D_{C}^{-}$\end{document} terms becomes:(A1.41)12∑d∈DC+(Q(ωl,θd)Fd+Q(ωl,θd′)Fd′¯+Q(ωl,θd′)Fd′+Q(ωl,θd)Fd¯)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}\sum _{d \in D_C^+}\left (Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d} + \overline {Q(\omega _l, \theta {d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}}+ Q(\omega _{l}, \theta {d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}+ \overline {Q(\omega _l, \theta _d)\boldsymbol {F}_d}\right)$$\end{document}(A1.42)=12∑d∈DC+((QdFd+QdFd¯)+(Qd′Fd′+Qd′Fd′¯))\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \frac{1}{2}\sum _{d \in D_C^+}\left ((Q_{d}\boldsymbol {F}_{d} + \overline {Q_d\boldsymbol {F}_d}) + (Q{d'}\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}+ \overline {Q{d'}\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}}) \right)$$\end{document}(A1.43)=∑d∈DC+Re[Q(ωl,θd)Fd]+∑d′∈DC−Re[Q(ωl,θd′)Fd′]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \sum _{d \in D_C^+}\text{Re}\left [Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d}\right ] + \sum _{d' \in D_C^-}\text{Re}\left [Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d'})\boldsymbol {F}_{d'}\right ]$$\end{document}

Combining this with the DR\begin{document}$D_{R}$\end{document} sum, which is ∑d∈DRRe[Q(ωl,0)Fd]\begin{document}$\sum _{d \in D_R}\text{Re}[Q(\omega _{l}, 0)\boldsymbol {F}_{d}]$\end{document}, we arrive at:(A1.44)∑d=1nRe[Q(ωl,θd)Fd]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sum _{d=1}^{n}\text{Re}\left [Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})\boldsymbol {F}_{d}\right ]$$\end{document}

This is the real part of the product of the terms Q(ωl,θd)\begin{document}$Q(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})$\end{document} and Fd\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {F}_{d}$\end{document} defined in Equations A1.28; A1.29. Therefore, the second term of the x(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}(t)$\end{document} can be expressed as:(A1.45)∑k=0t−1At−1−kB∑l=1Lcos⁡(ωlk)u0\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{\,t-1-k}\boldsymbol {B}\,\sum _{l=1}^{L}\cos (\omega _{l} k)\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$$\end{document}(A1.46)=∑l=1L∑d=1nRe[rdt+1eiθd(t−1)−rdtei(θdt−ωl)−rdei(ωlt−θd)+eiωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(θd−ωl)+1vdwd⊤Bu0],\begin{document}$$\displaystyle = \sum _{l=1}^{L}\sum _{d=1}^{n}\text{Re}\left [\frac{r_{d}^{t+1}e^{i\theta _d(t-1)}-r_{d}^{t}e^{i(\theta _dt-\omega _l)}-r_{d}e^{i(\omega _l t-\theta _d)}+e^{i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\theta _{d}-\omega _{l})+1}\boldsymbol {v}_{d} \boldsymbol {w}_{d}^{\top } \boldsymbol {B}\,\boldsymbol {u}_{0}\right ],$$\end{document}

Therefore, the state vector x(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}(t)$\end{document} is decomposed into a passive and a difference term as follows,(A1.47)x(t)=xpassive(t)+xdiff(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}(t) = \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{passive}}(t)+\boldsymbol {x}_{\text{diff}}(t),$$\end{document}(A1.48)xpassive(t)=Atx(0)+∑k=0t−1At−1−kξ(k)\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{passive}}(t) = \boldsymbol {A}^{t} \boldsymbol {x}(0) + \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {\xi }(k)$$\end{document}(A1.49)xdiff(t)=∑l=1L∑d=1nRe[rdt+1eiθd(t−1)−rdtei(θdt−ωl)−rdei(ωlt−θd)+eiωl(t−1)rd2−2rdcos⁡(θd−ωl)+1vdwd⊤Bu0]\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{diff}}(t) = \sum _{l=1}^{L}\sum _{d=1}^{n}\text{Re}\left [\frac{r_{d}^{t+1}e^{i\theta _d(t-1)}-r_{d}^{t}e^{i(\theta _dt-\omega _l)}-r_{d}e^{i(\omega _l t-\theta _d)}+e^{i\omega _l(t-1)}}{r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\theta _{d}-\omega _{l})+1}\boldsymbol {v}_{d} \boldsymbol {w}_{d}^{\top } \boldsymbol {B}\,\boldsymbol {u}_{0}\right ]$$\end{document}

where xpassive(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}_{\text{passive}}(t)$\end{document} represents the state x that would be realized if no perturbation were applied, i.e., the state that would evolve according to Equation 10 with u=0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}=0$\end{document} in the main text. xdiff(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}_{\text{diff}}(t)$\end{document} represents the change in the state trajectory induced by the specific perturbation input u(k)=∑l=1Lcos⁡(ωlk)u0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}(k) = \sum _{l=1}^{L}\cos (\omega _{l} k)\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$\end{document}. As defined in the previous section, λd=rdeiθd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d} = r_{d} e^{i\theta _d}$\end{document} is the polar form of the d-th eigenvalue, the vector vd\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {v}_{d}$\end{document} denotes the right eigenvector of A associated with λd\begin{document}$\lambda _{d}$\end{document}, and wd⊤\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {w}_{d}^{\top }$\end{document} denotes the corresponding left eigenvector. The numerator of the fraction in Equation A1.46 consists of four distinct oscillatory terms. The resonant behavior of this expression is primarily governed by the denominator, D(ωl,θd)=rd2−2rdcos⁡(θd−ωl)+1\begin{document}$D(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d}) = r_{d}^{2}-2r_{d}\cos (\theta _{d}-\omega _{l})+1$\end{document}. The gain term 1/D(ωl,θd)\begin{document}$1/D(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})$\end{document} has a single extremum (a maximum) with respect to ωl\begin{document}$\omega _{l}$\end{document}, which occurs when cos⁡(θd−ωl)=1\begin{document}$\cos (\theta _{d}-\omega _{l})=1$\end{document}, i.e., when the input frequency ωl\begin{document}$\omega _{l}$\end{document} matches the eigenfrequency (argument) θd\begin{document}$\theta _{d}$\end{document} of the system.

The restriction to a common spatial pattern u0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$\end{document} in the input u(k)=∑l=1Lcos⁡(ωlk)u0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}(k) = \sum _{l=1}^{L} \cos (\omega _{l} k)\,\boldsymbol {u}_{0}$\end{document} is a simplifying assumption made to present the theory of this paper clearly, and it can be naturally replaced by frequency-specific patterns ul\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}_{l}$\end{document}. The simplification keeps the formulation consistent with the impulse and step inputs, and it isolates the effect of the input frequencies from that of the stimulation location, thereby keeping the presentation in the main text intuitive. Substituting u0→ul\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}_{0} \to \boldsymbol {u}_{l}$\end{document} gives a more general expression, but it leaves the denominator D(ωl,θd)\begin{document}$D(\omega _{l}, \theta _{d})$\end{document} untouched, so the conclusion that the input frequencies should match the mode frequencies is unchanged. Optimization that also includes the stimulation location can be carried out by numerically minimizing Equation A1.14, so the practical estimation procedure and design strategy remain unchanged.

sec.title: Appendix 1.2.2 Impulse and step input
sec.p: Impulse and step inputs follow simple rules. Let α represent the scaling factor for impulse input. Then, input u(k)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}(k)$\end{document} is defined as:(A1.50)u(k)={αu0if k=0,0if k>0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {u}(k) = \begin{cases} \alpha \boldsymbol {u}_{0}&\text{if }k = 0, \\ 0&\text{if }k \gt 0. \end{cases}$$\end{document}

Here, u0∈Rm\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$\end{document} represents the fundamental input direction applied to the system, determining which input channel receives the impulse. We obtain the decomposition:(A1.51)xpassive(t)=Atx(0)+∑k=0t−1At−1−kξ(k),xdiff(t)=αAt−1Bu0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{passive}}(t) = \boldsymbol {A}^{t}\boldsymbol {x}(0)+\sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {\xi }(k),\quad \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{diff}}(t) = \alpha \boldsymbol {A}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}_{0}.$$\end{document}

For a scaled step input, u(k)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {u}(k)$\end{document} is defined as(A1.52)u(k)=βu0,∀k≥0,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {u}(k) = \beta \boldsymbol {u}_{0}, \quad \forall k \geq 0,$$\end{document}

where β is the input strength. We then get the decomposition:(A1.53)xpassive(t)=Atx(0)+∑k=0t−1At−1−kξ(k),xdiff(t)=β∑k=0t−1At−1−kBu0.\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{passive}}(t) = \boldsymbol {A}^{t}\boldsymbol {x}(0)+\sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {\xi }(k),\quad \boldsymbol {x}_{\text{diff}}(t) = \beta \sum _{k=0}^{t-1}\boldsymbol {A}^{t-1-k}\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}_{0}.$$\end{document}

From these solutions, we can infer that the input-driven terms (xdiff(t)\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {x}_{\text{diff}}(t)$\end{document}) are linear in the input strengths α and β. Consequently, the contribution of these inputs to the state covariance matrix (i.e. the outer product of the state vector) will scale quadratically with α2\begin{document}$\alpha ^{2}$\end{document} and β2\begin{document}$\beta ^{2}$\end{document}. This analysis, which suggests that such inputs can increase the rank or magnitude of the covariance matrix eigenvalues, is explored further in the main text.

sec.title: 2.1 Simulation details
sec.p: The specific conditions used for generating neural dynamics in each section are summarized in Appendix 2—table 1. These include factors, such as sampling frequency, trial length, and perturbation input strength, which are crucial for designing reproducible simulations and evaluations. These parameters are chosen to illustrate the theoretical insights as clearly as possible, rather than to characterise the framework’s behaviour across generic regimes.

sec.title: 2.2 Robustness to nonlinear state dynamics
sec.p: We introduce nonlinearity into the state update by replacing the linear update with a nonlinear function of the current state,(A2.1)x(t+1)=Aβtanh(βx(t))+Bu(t)+ξ(t),\begin{document}$$\displaystyle \boldsymbol {x}(t{+}1)=\frac{\boldsymbol {A}}{\beta }\,\tanh \!\bigl (\beta \,\boldsymbol {x}(t)\bigr)+\boldsymbol {B}\boldsymbol {u}(t)+\boldsymbol {\xi }(t),$$\end{document}

on a 4-dimensional two-mode network, which is the extended setup of Figure 2. The detailed parameters are given in Appendix 2—table 1. The 1/β\begin{document}$1/\beta$\end{document} prefactor normalises the dynamics. The tanh\begin{document}$\tanh $\end{document} function is a common choice for introducing nonlinearity (Khalil, 2002) while maintaining bounded outputs, and the parameter β controls the degree of nonlinearity (Appendix 2—figure 1a). Because the true map is now nonlinear in x, a direct comparison of A^\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}$\end{document} against the true A is no longer well-defined; we, therefore, evaluate the misspecified linear OLS estimator by the relative one-step prediction RMSE and the relative free-run (rollout) RMSE.

Under both metrics, the impulse condition tracks the true dynamics more accurately than passive observation across the swept range, with the gap shrinking when β grows large enough that the nonlinearity itself re-excites the 40 Hz hidden mode strongly (Appendix 2—figure 1b and c). Appendix 2—figure 1d and e show the time series for the passive and impulse conditions across the range of β, illustrating that the impulse condition strongly excites the mode dynamics. Appendix 2—figure 1f and g compare the true and predicted time series; under both error metrics, the impulse condition tracks the true dynamics more accurately than passive observation. Appendix 2—figure 1h shows the top three principal components of the data. Even when nonlinearity is present in the dynamics, the impulse condition still re-excites the hidden mode (third PC) and yields better predictions than passive observation.

sec.title: 2.3 Joint estimation of A and B
sec.p: The naive estimator that assumes B=I\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {B}=\boldsymbol {I}$\end{document} absorbs the unmodelled term (Btrue−I)u\begin{document}$(\boldsymbol {B}_{\mathrm{true}}-\boldsymbol {I})\boldsymbol {u}$\end{document} into A^\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}$\end{document}, so its error in A grows with the mismatch level ε=‖Btrue−I‖F\begin{document}$\varepsilon =\|\boldsymbol {B}_{\mathrm{true}}-\boldsymbol {I}\|_{F}$\end{document}. A natural remedy is to estimate A and B jointly by regressing the next state on the stacked [X;U]\begin{document}$[\boldsymbol {X};\boldsymbol {U}]$\end{document} block,(A2.2)[A^,B^]=X+[X−;U]†,\begin{document}$$\displaystyle [\hat {\boldsymbol {A}},\,\hat {\boldsymbol {B}}] \;=\; \boldsymbol {X}_{+}\;[\boldsymbol {X}_{-};\,\boldsymbol {U}]^{\dagger },$$\end{document}

which is unbiased whenever the input excites every state coordinate. We compare seven conditions on a 4-dimensional, 2-mode discrete-time system: the ground truth; passive observation; joint estimation under four perturbation patterns, with input on (i) node 1 alone, (ii) node 3 alone, (iii) nodes 1 and 3, and (iv) all four nodes; and a baseline that uses the all-nodes input but estimates A under the naive assumption B^=I\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {B}}=\boldsymbol {I}$\end{document}. The true matrix uses the same setup as Figure 2. The detailed parameters are given in Appendix 2—table 1. Every stimulated trial uses 4 impulses whose amplitudes on the active channels are drawn independently from N(0,I)\begin{document}$\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol {I})$\end{document} per pulse, so that the rank of the U-block of the regressor equals min(nactive,4)\begin{document}$\min (n_{\mathrm{active}}, 4)$\end{document}. We parametrise the mismatch as Btrue=I+εR\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {B}_{\mathrm{true}}=\boldsymbol {I}+\varepsilon \boldsymbol {R}$\end{document} with a fixed random matrix R normalised so that ‖R‖F=1\begin{document}$\|\boldsymbol {R}\|_{F}=1$\end{document}, which makes ε the scalar control parameter for the sweep.

The results show that the perturbation can still improve the estimation of A even when B is unknown, provided that A and B are recovered jointly by OLS. In the joint-estimation results of Appendix 2—figure 2a, only the columns of B corresponding to the stimulated channels are recovered: the (1, 3) pattern fills two columns, and the all-nodes pattern recovers B to the accuracy attainable when B is known. Nevertheless, A can be estimated correctly, including its hidden dynamical mode. The third column of the same panel shows that the naive estimator under the assumption B^=I\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {B}}=\boldsymbol {I}$\end{document} recovers A only approximately. Appendix 2—figure 2b shows the corresponding state trajectories. Appendix 2—figure 2c shows ‖A−A^‖F\begin{document}$\|\boldsymbol {A}-\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}\|_{F}$\end{document} as ε is swept on a log scale. Passive observation is pinned at the hidden-mode bias, and the naive B^=I\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {B}}=\boldsymbol {I}$\end{document} baseline grows with ε as the unmodelled (Btrue−I)ut\begin{document}$(\boldsymbol {B}_{\mathrm{true}}-\boldsymbol {I})\boldsymbol {u}_{t}$\end{document} term inflates the residual variance. Among the joint estimators, stimulating node 1 alone yields an intermediate error because node 1 is not directly coupled to the hidden mode; stimulating node 3 yields a markedly lower error because node 3 excites the hidden mode and thereby renders it identifiable; and stimulating all nodes is better still, matching the error achievable when B is known. The (1, 3) pattern lies between the node 3 and all-nodes cases. The error ‖B−B^‖F\begin{document}$\|\boldsymbol {B}-\hat {\boldsymbol {B}}\|_{F}$\end{document} grows linearly with ε for the rank-deficient stimulation patterns and the naive baseline, and matches the known-B baseline only for the all-nodes pattern under joint OLS. Although these results provide only a preliminary demonstration of the robustness of the proposed framework, joint estimation of A and B is a promising direction for future work to relax the assumption of known B.

sec.title: 2.4 Demonstration of impulse and step input
sec.p: Impulse- and step-like inputs, such as those applied in TMS or tDCS, can substantially improve system identification accuracy when applied at high intensities. By perturbing the system state further from equilibrium, the resulting decay dynamics provide richer trajectory information. This richer information increases the eigenvalues of the state covariance matrix and, in turn, reduces estimation error.

The relationship between input intensity and system identification accuracy was examined through simulations using matrix A, as illustrated in Appendix 2—figure 3a. For the dynamics generated by matrix A, system identification was performed using impulse and step inputs of varying intensities. As shown in Appendix 2—figure 3b and c, the identification error decreases exponentially as the input intensity increases. This error was observed to be inversely correlated with the sum of the inverses of the eigenvalues of the state covariance matrix. In practice, the strength of perturbation input must be constrained within the limits allowed by experimental conditions. However, our findings indicate that perturbation inputs should be designed to be as strong as possible within biologically acceptable ranges.

sec.title: 2.5 White noise vs. concatenated frequency input

caption.title: Comparison between white noise input and optimized frequency input.
caption.p: (a) Matrix A with 16 modes, assuming 32 channels. (b) Channel-averaged power spectrum in the passive state. (c) Comparison of the sum of reciprocal eigenvalues (∑i(1/μi)\begin{document}$\sum _{i} (1/\mu _{i})$\end{document}) of the covariance matrix of the state vector under white noise and optimized frequency input. (d) Comparison of eigenvalue-scaled ellipsoids obtained from white noise and optimized frequency input, visualizing the components corresponding to the 1st–3rd and 30th–32nd eigenvalues.

sec.p: We demonstrate both the effectiveness and suboptimality of white noise input for neural system identification, a standard approach widely used in control engineering (Goodwin and Payne, 1977; Ljung, 1999). White noise contains a broad and nearly uniform range of frequencies, making it a convenient and practical choice for identifying system models when no prior information is available. However, as discussed in the main text, the input should ideally be designed to match the dynamical modes of the system. Thus, we consider white noise input as a practical yet potentially suboptimal method for neural system identification.

To assess the feasibility of the white noise perturbation input, we assume that a neural perturbation system is capable of generating random noise-like signals and that these input signals can be recorded simultaneously. We generated 32-channel time-series data using the matrix A shown in Appendix 2—figure 4a. Data were generated at sampling rate fs=100\begin{document}$f_{s} = 100$\end{document} Hz, with total length T=10,000\begin{document}$T = 10,000$\end{document} samples. The system matrix A∈R32×32\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {A}\in \mathbb{R}^{32\times 32}$\end{document} was constructed as the block diagonal of 16 discrete-time 2×2 rotation blocks whose eigenvalue radii were drawn from Unif(0.9,0.95)\begin{document}$\mathrm{Unif}(0.9,\,0.95)$\end{document} and modal frequencies from Unif(1,100)\begin{document}$\mathrm{Unif}(1,\,100)$\end{document} Hz. The system dynamics exhibit multiple modes, as shown in Appendix 2—figure 4b. The input matrix was B=I32\begin{document}$\boldsymbol {B}= \boldsymbol {I}_{32}$\end{document} with single-node stimulation applied through its first column. Process noise was i.i.d. Gaussian with per-component standard deviation σξ=10−2\begin{document}$\sigma _{\xi } = 10^{-2}$\end{document}. The designed input was a sinusoidal input with frequencies matching the modal frequencies of the system, which were extracted from the eigenvalues of A. Starting from white noise, the modal frequencies {ωk}\begin{document}$\{\omega _{k}\}$\end{document} extracted from the eigenvalues of A^\begin{document}$\hat {\boldsymbol {A}}$\end{document} were used as the component frequencies of the next input (design-1), and this redesign was iterated twice more (design-2, design-3). To ensure a fair comparison, both the white noise and the designed inputs were normalized to have the same total input power. This setup allows for a controlled comparison between white noise input and frequency-optimized input.

The system identification error decreased when using frequency-designed inputs rather than white noise. Appendix 2—figure 4c shows the sum of reciprocal eigenvalues (∑i(1/μi)\begin{document}$\sum _{i} (1/\mu _{i})$\end{document}) of the covariance matrix of the state vectors. This value decreased when using frequency-designed inputs rather than white noise, indicating improved accuracy in system identification. Moreover, iterative redesigns progressively reduced the sum of reciprocal eigenvalues (designs 2 and 3), leading to more accurate identification. As shown in Appendix 2—figure 4d, both white noise and designed concatenated frequency inputs excited all dynamical modes without collapsing the smaller axes. The ellipsoids obtained with the designed input had smaller volumes, indicating higher identification accuracy. Therefore, this simulation demonstrates that iterative optimal design can yield more accurate system identification than conventional white noise stimulation.

In summary, white noise input offers a simple and practical strategy for neural system identification when no prior dynamical information is available. Nevertheless, it remains suboptimal compared with concatenated frequency input, which provides higher accuracy and stability through iterative refinement. These findings also highlight the importance of input optimization in achieving precise system identification in complex neural systems.

body.p: This important study introduces a method, based on active control, for determining the functional connectivity between neurons or groups of neurons. While the theory is derived for a linear model with a perfectly observed control signal, the authors present compelling evidence that their method will work even when the system is nonlinear and the control signal is not fully observed. Furthermore, they provide a practical recipe for doing so.
Summary:

Inferring so-called "functional connectivity" between neurons or groups of neurons is important both for validating models and for inferring brain state, including in human patients. This study aims to enhance this inference process by using closed-loop perturbation-based approaches. To this end, the authors develop a framework based on linear dynamical models that minimizes the estimation error. Based on this framework, the authors provide a practical guide for applying it in realistic experiments. Modalities include non-invasive ones, such as fMRI, iEEG, and invasive ones, such as optogenetic perturbations combined with neuropixel probes or calcium imaging.
Strengths:

A main strength of this paper is the application and adaptation of an explicit error expression to system dynamics estimation from evoked neural responses, bringing a useful theoretical tool into computational neuroscience for, as far as we know, the first time. Importantly, while the analytical derivation assumes the neural dynamics is linear and the control signal is known, these assumptions do not appear to be essential: their method outperforms passive observation even when the true dynamics is nonlinear or the control input is not known perfectly. Moreover, the relative simplicity of the method makes its practical applications straightforward, as the authors illustrate in the context of brain state classification and neural control.

Besides being of practical importance, simply pointing out that passive observation can lead to large mis-estimation of functional connectivity should serve as a wakeup call to anybody engaged in this endeavor.
Weaknesses:
None.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

We thank the reviewers for this careful observation. This concern is associated with the error term. Thus, we first clarified the noise assumption explicitly. We assume that ξ(t) is i.i.d. over time with zero mean and an arbitrary (not necessarily diagonal) positive definite covariance matrix Σξ=E[ξ(t)ξ(t)⊤]∈Rn×n≻0\begin{document}$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\xi}=\mathbb{E}\left[\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) \boldsymbol{\xi}(t)^{\top}\right] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \succ 0$\end{document}.

In particular, factorisation of the covariance into noise and the inverse of the observation covariance matrix needs a more thorough justification. The cited sources do not contain the derivation for a noise term with full covariance, which is essential for deriving this error term.

The cited sources do contain the derivation for a noise term with full covariance. We have updated the citation that directly supports Eq. (S.2): Proposition 11.1 of Hamilton (1994, TimeSeries Analysis), which establishes the asymptotic distribution Tvec⁡(Π^T−π)→LN(0,Ω⊗Q−1)\begin{document}$\sqrt{T} \operatorname{vec}\left(\hat{\mathbf{\Pi}}_{T}-\pi\right) \xrightarrow{L} \mathcal{N}\left(0, \Omega \otimes Q^{-1}\right)$\end{document} The proof, given in Appendix 11.A of Hamilton (1994), proceeds via a CLT for martingale difference sequences. body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding model mis-specification. We agree that it is important to run simulations to assess the impact of these model mismatches, therefore we conducted preliminary simulations to assess the sensitivity when two primary assumptions are violated: linear state dynamics and a perfectly known input matrix B. We added these preliminary results in the Supplementary Material, and revised the main manuscript to include a mention of these results. In summary, the simulations showed:

The model estimation error increases with the strength of the nonlinearity; however, perturbation can increase the information and lead to accurate estimation of the hidden mode even under nonlinearity.
The matrix A can be estimated roughly even if the assumed input matrix B differs from the true matrix in some cases.
The matrices A and B can be estimated jointly without bias, provided the stimulation pattern excites the full state space.

In such joint estimation, preferentially exciting the hidden modes directly leads to more accurate estimation of A than stimulating other modes. See Background and Results - Main Manuscript, Experimental Conditions and Results - Supplementary Material.

body.p: The accuracy and range of control inputs vary substantially depending on the specific stimulation technique and experimental setup, and a thorough discussion would require a dedicated review beyond the scope of this manuscript. Instead, we have added a sentence acknowledging the gap between practical experimental implementations and the theoretical formulation, and cited relevant references for readers interested in further details.
Background - Main Manuscript
“Neural Stimulation as Control Inputs

This section describes how commonly used neural stimulation techniques can be related to input signals in control theory. Their adjustable parameters vary depending on how the stimulation inputs are modulated.

Three non-invasive electrical stimulation methods illustrate how stimulation paradigms map onto basic control inputs. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) induces brief and transient perturbations via electromagnetic pulses [19], which are naturally represented as a sequence of impulse-like inputs, where the timing and intensity of each pulse are the primary controllable parameters. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) primarily modulates neural activity through approximately constant inputs [26], which can be viewed as a step-like signal whose main controllable parameter is the amplitude of the applied current. Transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) delivers oscillatory inputs [7], corresponding to sinusoidal signals characterized by amplitude, frequency, and phase. In control theory, impulse, step, and sinusoidal inputs are the basic components used to characterize system responses and dynamics [22, 21].

The control input framework extends beyond non-invasive techniques to invasive and optogenetic stimulation. Invasive electrical stimulation, including intracranial microstimulation and deep brain stimulation (DBS), enables direct delivery of electrical inputs to neural tissue [17], providing flexible control over amplitude and timing through pulse trains or temporally structured waveforms. Optogenetic stimulation allows genetically targeted activation or inhibition of specific neurons using light [5], providing fine-grained control over multiple input dimensions, including amplitude (light intensity), temporal pattern, and cell-type specificity. In particular, recent developments enable stimulation at the level of individual neurons with high temporal precision [27, 16], allowing flexible construction of spatiotemporal input patterns.

These stimulation examples demonstrate that the theoretical framework developed in this paper connects to practical experimental settings. While a substantial gap remains between idealized control inputs in theory and experimentally realizable stimulation, the core principles established in the following sections provide a foundation that naturally extends to these practical stimulation paradigms.”

disp-quote.p: What are the physical units for the time scales and stimulation amplitudes?

This study is a theoretical investigation that focuses on the relative differences between passive observation and perturbation-based approaches, rather than providing precise predictions for specific experimental settings. The time scales and stimulation amplitudes are therefore expressed in arbitrary units.

disp-quote.p: For instance, on page 13, there is an argument that "In practical experiments, such long windows are unrealistic because neural states change rapidly over time." However, it is unclear whether T=100 a.u. or T=1000 a.u. etc. is realistic.

Results - Main Manuscript

“To obtain estimates under the passive condition that are comparable to those derived under perturbation, it is necessary to experimentally observe extensive time-series data. Figure 7f illustrates the LDA projection and classification accuracy for different time-series lengths. We have revised the impulse amplitude from 1020 to 102, as 1020 is physically unrealistic—it would imply a stimulus intensity many orders of magnitude beyond any conceivable experimental setting. The revised value of 102 is more plausible: for reference, TMS stimulation voltages exceed typical EEG amplitudes by roughly 4–6 orders of magnitude. The classification accuracy decreased slightly; however, our main conclusion regarding the efficiency of the perturbation-based approach under limited data remains unchanged. See Table B.1.

disp-quote.p: (15) Strongly perturbing/Exciting fast-decaying modes to give them more ’runway’ and increase observed variability makes intuitive sense for a normal system. But what would happen in the case of non-normal dynamics, where stimulating one dimension only transiently amplifies it, but then excites other dimensions? Non-normality breaks the alignment between PC components and dynamic modes (see Kumar, Ankit, Loren M. Frank, and Kristofer E. Bouchard. "Identifying feedforward and feedback controllable subspaces of neural population dynamics." arXiv preprint arXiv:2408.05875 (2024)), so eigenvectors of A and ΣX won’t align for non-normal dynamics. This alignment appears to be a hidden assumption of this paper. Should the normal dynamics then be stated as an assumption/limitation of the framework? Is the example in Figure 6a highly non-normal? Does considering out-degree provide an empirical approach, an alternative to ’enlargement’, to dealing with non-normality?

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment regarding non-normal dynamics.

disp-quote.p: Should normal dynamics be stated as an assumption/limitation of the framework?

body.p: No. Our framework does not assume normal dynamics. For example, Figure 5 and the revised Figure 6 illustrate non-normal cases. In Figure 5, the row and column norms of A differ substantially (row norms ≈ [1.96, 4.05, 1.33, 4.70]; column norms ≈ [6.14, 1.94, 1.39, 0.87]). In Figure 6, Node 7 is a hub with only outgoing edges, so row 7 of A is zero while column 7 has nonzero entries. In addition, the Nodes 5–6 and Nodes 3–4 are strictly one-way, leaving the corresponding off-diagonal block upper-triangular. Both features break the symmetry required for normality.

We additionally computed a commutator-based non-normality index ‖AA⊤−A⊤A‖F/‖A‖F2\begin{document}$\left\|\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{A}^{\top}-\boldsymbol{A}^{\top} \boldsymbol{A}\right\|_{F} /\|\boldsymbol{A}\|_{F}^{2}$\end{document} which equals 0 for any normal matrix and approaches 2≈1.41\begin{document}$\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$\end{document} for the canonical maximally non-normal example (the 2×2 nilpotent Jordan block). The non-normality index is 1.34 for Figure 5 and 0.41 for Figure 6. These values confirm that both are clearly non-normal.

disp-quote.p: Is the example in Figure 6a highly non-normal?

body.p: Yes. As stated above, the network structure of Figure 6a clearly indicates non-normality.

disp-quote.p: Does considering out-degree provide an empirical approach, an alternative to ‘enlargement’, to dealing with non-normality?

body.p: No. In the previous manuscript, the results of out-degree and eigenvector structure were provided as supplementary intuition. However, the central contribution of our framework lies in maximizing the minimum eigenvalue µ of the observed state covariance (Equation 9), and for systems where non-normality is strong and subnetwork structure is less modular, the iterative optimization of tr⁡[ΣX−1]\begin{document}$\operatorname{tr}\left[\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\boldsymbol{X}}^{-1}\right]$\end{document} provides a principled, assumption-free method. We clearly mentioned this point in the revised manuscript as follows. See Results in the main manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (18) Is it reasonable to assume full observability of the system? It would be interesting to consider biases arising from the partial observability of the system, in the spirit of Figure 9, which looked at partial controllability.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We agree that partial observability is an important consideration, however it is out of scope for the current work. Thus, we have added a future direction in the Discussion addressing partial observability. We note that Takens’ embedding theorem and Hankel DMD enable recovery of a system’s eigenvalues from partial observations, and since our framework relies on the eigenvalue structure of A, the proposed perturbation design remains applicable under partial observability.
Discussion - Main Manuscript

“Two directions warrant further investigation: extending the framework to partial observability, and validating it through stimulation experiments. In experimental neuroscience, recordings are often limited to a subset of neural populations, resulting in partial observability. A growing body of work has leveraged delay-embedding techniques, represented by Takens’ embedding theorem [25], to reconstruct hidden dynamics from partial observations [2, 3, 23, 11]. Applying such techniques enables the estimation of the full connectivity matrix, thereby extending our framework to settings with partial observability. The second direction concerns experimental validation. Validating a theoretical framework through experimental design is an essential in bridging the gap between theory and practice.”

Introduction - Main Manuscript

“In this paper, we propose a framework for designing the optimal perturbation input through control theory in neuroscience. We interpret neural dynamics as a control system [8, 6, 14, 12, 20, 24], and treat external perturbations as control inputs to design properties of neural stimulation (Fig. 1d). If the optimal perturbation input can be systematically designed, it becomes possible to steer the neural system toward states that are maximally informative (Fig. 1e), thereby enhancing the accuracy of the inferred connectivity (Fig. 1f). While recent studies have begun to develop algorithmic approaches to active stimulation design for specific experimental platforms [18, 28], a general theoretical framework for why and which perturbation inputs are effective has yet to be established. We first describe how to formulate neural dynamics as a control system and how to estimate the model parameters from observed data. Building upon this formulation, we derive a theoretical basis that enables us to design the optimal perturbation inputs for the neural system identification. We demonstrate the validity and utility of this theoretical basis by exploring its implications for optimizing parameters of common neurostimulation techniques and by applying it to practical examples, including neural state classification [4, 9, 1, 24] and control of neural states [8, 13, 14, 12]. In these demonstrations, we define concrete problems and apply the theory to validate its practical utility.”
